title: The Darkest Night

pages.text:
*The Fourteenth Rule of Mapmaking: On the darkest night, draw the smallest line.*

The fire popped, spitting orange sparks into the dark. Around them, the world was black and silent, save for the distant, rhythmic thrum of the sea far below the cliff edge. Tam sat on a flat rock, her knees drawn up to her chin. She had the sum written out in her head, and she had checked it twice, and both times the answer was the same: not enough time.

Lucan’s team had vanished into the night, their lanterns bobbing like distant, confused stars as they searched for the old road back to Verrin. That left Tam and Odd with the Hollow Cliffs. Two days’ work. Four days left.

Odd did not look at her. He sat by the fire, poking a knot with a stick, sending up a thin trail of white smoke. His red hair was matted with ash, and his gap-toothed grin was gone, replaced by a tight, serious line. He knew the math. He always knew the math. He just knew it differently than she did, perhaps, because for him, the distance was measured in miles, and for her, it was measured in lines she hadn’t drawn yet.

Tam watched the smoke curl upward and disappear. The air was cold, biting at her nose, carrying the sharp, salty scent of the cliffs. She looked at her hands, ink-stained and trembling slightly, and wished they were somewhere else. Anywhere but here, on this rock, staring at the impossible.
pages.image: A sturdy 11-year-old girl with a black braid and ink-stained fingers sits on a rock by a small fire, staring at a gangly red-haired boy poking the flames with a stick; dark cliff edge and distant sea in the background.

pages.text:
Tam dragged her satchel close, the leather creaking against her chest. Inside, the maps lay in a damp, crumpled heap, their ink smudged into unreadable blots. But her mind kept pulling her back to Lucan’s charts. They were neat. They were precise. They were perfect.

She pictured the gold compass swinging on his chain, catching the firelight, and a heavy, cold weight settled in her stomach. It felt exactly like the feeling she had every time she watched the Academy apprentices draw straight lines with the ease of tying their boots.

*You began too far behind,* the old whisper hissed, quiet and familiar. *You learned your letters at nine. You draw crooked lines. You will never catch up.*

It was a lie, she knew. Yet the tightness in her throat suggested it might be true.

She glanced at Odd. He was still poking the fire, his red hair matted with ash, his gap-toothed grin replaced by a serious, tight line. He didn’t offer comfort. He didn’t try to fix the problem. He simply sat there, solid as a dock piling, letting the silence hang in the cold air.

"I'm not going to make it," Tam said. Her voice sounded thin, scraped raw by the wind. "I've done the sums, Odd. Twice. It's not possible."

Odd stopped his stick. He looked at her, eyes wide and dark, then back at the flames. He didn’t argue. He didn’t say it would be fine. He just sat, and the fire crackled, and the night stretched out before them, long and dark and waiting.
pages.image: A close-up of a girl's face looking down with heavy eyes, next to a boy's profile staring into a fire; the background is dark and blurry, focusing on their solemn expressions and the warm glow of the flames.

pages.text:
A soft thump landed on the fire-ring stones. Tam flinched, then froze. It was Sixpence, her grey pigeon with the white patch on her chest, panting, her feathers ruffled and damp. Tied to her leg was a small, rolled tube of waxed cloth.

Tam untied it with shaking fingers. Her breath came in short, sharp bursts. She unrolled the paper. Master Finch’s handwriting was there, shaky but clear.

*My hands will not hold a straight line, Tam. I tremble. I am losing the trade to age. But this is not a tragedy. It is a season.*

Tam read on, her eyes stinging. Finch wrote of her first map, the one that was a disaster, the one she had hidden in a drawer for years. *I was not trying to be the best mapmaker in Aldermere. I was trying to be a better one than I had been the day before. I have been doing that for sixty years. It has been enough.*

The words floated in the firelight, warm and steady. Tam looked at the trembling hand she held the paper with, and then at her own. The fear was still there, but it was smaller now. Smaller, like a knot in a rope coming loose under steady pressure.
pages.image: A small grey pigeon with a white chest patch stands on a stone near a fire, while a girl's hands hold a rolled piece of paper; the background is dark, illuminated only by the fire's glow.

pages.text:
The letter ended with a final instruction. *Tonight you cannot draw the whole map. Draw one small line. Tomorrow, draw another. That is all of it.*

Tam read it once, then twice, letting the words settle deep into her bones before folding the paper carefully and tucking it into her coat. She pulled out her Yesterday Book, the leather soft and worn from months of handling. Uncapping her ink pot, the sharp, familiar smell of oak-gall rose to meet her nose. She dipped her quill, and to her surprise, her hand was steady.

She drew the river, that same wobbling stripe with two bends in the middle. It was small, and it was simple, but it was the straightest line she had ever managed. Beneath it, in tiny, careful letters, she wrote: *Dark night. Small line. Better.*

Odd read it over her shoulder. He did not smile, and he did not say it was good. He simply watched her for a long moment, then looked away, giving her the quiet space she needed. It was the kindest thing he could have done, and Tam felt the tension loosen in her chest, like a tight knot finally coming undone under steady pressure.
pages.image: A girl's hand holding a quill over a small open notebook, drawing a simple line; a boy's face is visible in the background, watching quietly; firelight illuminates their faces and hands.

pages.text:
Tam closed the book.

The night was deep, and the stars hung above the cliffs like cold, hard buttons sewn onto a vast, dark coat. The wind picked up, whistling through the rocks with a sound that was almost rude. It carried the crash of the sea against the Hollow Cliffs, a steady, thumping rhythm that vibrated in Tam's teeth.

She took a deep breath. The air tasted of salt and peat. She looked out past the fire, past the jagged edge of the stone, to the distant, glowing city of Verrin. The lights there were far away, small and steady, like the eyes of sleeping cats.

"I'm not too far behind," she said. Her voice was quiet, but it did not waver. "I'm exactly where I am. And tomorrow I'll be one line further."

The wind blew. The stars wheeled slowly in their tracks.

Tam leaned back against the rock. The fire threw a warm, orange patch across her face, while the rest of her stood in the cool, blue dark. Her bones ached from the walk, a deep, honest tiredness that settled into her muscles. But the heavy knot in her stomach was gone. She closed her eyes and listened to the sea, counting the waves until the counting turned into sleep.
pages.image: A girl sleeps with her head tilted back against a rock, eyes closed; a boy sits nearby watching her; above them, a starry sky and the silhouette of dark cliffs against a distant, glowing horizon.
